summary: Describes two LDAPv3 control extensions for server-side sorting of search results. A client names the attribute types and matching rules the server should use when returning results. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of getting a pile of directory search results and sorting them itself, an LDAP client can ask the server to hand them over already in order. RFC 2891 defines the request that names the sort order and the reply that says whether the server managed to sort. If no reply control arrives, the client should assume nothing was sorted.

questions: what is ldap server side sorting
how does the ldap sort control work
what happens if an ldap server cannot sort results
subtitle: How an LDAP client asks the directory server to hand back search results already sorted.

tldr.problem: Some LDAP clients are too limited to sort search results themselves, or otherwise cannot, but still need the entries in a particular order.
tldr.mechanism: The client adds a request control listing sort keys (attribute type, optional matching rule, optional reverse flag) to its search. The server answers with a response control carrying a sort result code.
tldr.outcome: The client can trust the order only when the response control says success. If the control is absent, the client should assume the sort was ignored.

today: RFC 2891 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends LDAPv3 (RFC 2251).

sections.title: Two Controls for Sorted Results
sections.content:
RFC 2891 defines two LDAPv3 controls, which are extra pieces of data attached to an LDAP message. Together they let a client say which attribute types and matching rules a server should use when it returns the results of a search. The RFC says this may be useful when the client has limited functionality or otherwise cannot sort the results but still needs them sorted.

The pair is a request control, sent with the search in the searchRequest message, and a response control, returned with the final searchResultDone message. Because the response control carries its own result code, the server can report how the sorting went independently of the result code for the search itself. Other controls that may appear on searches are not defined here.
sections.plainLanguage: You hand the directory a note saying how to line the results up. The directory sends back a note saying whether it worked.

sections.title: The Request Control
sections.content:
The request control rides in the controls field of the searchRequest message. Its controlType is 1.2.840.113556.1.4.473. The client may set criticality to TRUE or FALSE; an absent value counts as FALSE. The controlValue is the BER encoding of a SortKeyList, a sequence of keys.

Each key has an attributeType, an optional orderingRule (a matching rule id) and a reverseOrder flag that defaults to FALSE. The list runs from highest to lowest sort key precedence.

  • The matching rule SHOULD be valid for its attribute type, otherwise the server returns inappropriateMatching.
  • If the ordering rule is omitted, the ordering matching rule defined for the attribute MUST be used.
  • An attribute type should appear only once; if it appears more than once, the server should return unwillingToPerform.
  • Any conformant implementation MUST allow a sort key list with at least one key.
sections.plainLanguage: The request lists the fields to sort by, in order of importance. Each field may name the rule for comparing values and whether to reverse that field's order.

sections.title: The Response Control and Result Codes
sections.content:
The response control is included in the searchResultDone message. Its controlType is 1.2.840.113556.1.4.474. Its criticality is FALSE and may be absent. The controlValue is the BER encoding of a SEQUENCE holding a sortResult code and an optional attributeType.

The code success (0) means the results are sorted. Other codes explain failures: timeLimitExceeded (3), strongAuthRequired (8, refused to return sorted results over an insecure protocol), adminLimitExceeded (11, too many entries to sort), noSuchAttribute (16), inappropriateMatching (18), insufficientAccessRights (50), busy (51), unwillingToPerform (53) and other (80).

On an error, the server MAY set attributeType to the first attribute type in the list that was at fault. The client SHOULD ignore that field when the result is success.
sections.plainLanguage: The reply note has a number for how it went: 0 means sorted, and other numbers explain what went wrong. It may also point at the first item on the list that caused the trouble.

sections.title: The Six Scenarios
sections.content:
The server SHOULD return all results for the search in the order given by the sort keys, reversed per key when reverseOrder is TRUE. The RFC lists six cases that depend on whether the server supports the control, whether it can sort with the given keys, and whether the client marked the control critical.

  • Unsupported, critical: the server MUST return unavailableCriticalExtension in searchResultDone and send no other results.
  • Unsupported, not critical: the server MUST ignore the control and process the search as if it were not present.
  • Supported but cannot sort, critical: the server SHOULD return unavailableCriticalExtension, include the response control and send no entries.
  • Supported but cannot sort, not critical: the server returns all results unsorted and includes the response control.
  • Can sort: the server includes the response control with a sort result of success.
  • Search failed or returned no entries: the server SHOULD omit the response control.

The client is assured of the order if and only if the result code is success. If the response control is omitted, the client SHOULD assume the sort control was ignored. Servers may also limit how many keys they accept, such as only one.
sections.plainLanguage: If the server cannot sort, a client that marked the control critical receives nothing, and one that did not receives an unsorted list with a note. If there is no note at all, assume nothing was sorted.

sections.title: Chaining, Missing Keys and Paged Results
sections.content:
If a server chains the request to other servers and the client set the criticality of the sort control to TRUE, the server MUST merge sort the results before returning them or MUST return unwillingToPerform.

An entry missing one or more sort keys is treated as having a value of NULL for that key, and NULL is considered larger than all other valid values. With one key, entries missing it collate after all others, or before all others if reverseOrder is set. If a sort key is a multi-valued attribute and no other controls affect the order, the server SHOULD use the least value according to the attribute's ordering rule.

When combined with the paged results control from RFC 2696, the server should sort the entire result set, not each page separately. The sort key list must be present on every search request for the page and must not change. The server SHOULD send the response control on every page so clients can tell quickly whether the set is sorted.
sections.plainLanguage: Results that have no value for a sort field go at the end of the line. If the results come in pages, the whole set is sorted first, not each page on its own.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Allowing sorting can let a client retrieve a large number of records from a directory despite administrative limits on how many records a search may return. A client that wants every record could combine sorting with updated search filters to pull the whole database out in small result sets, circumventing administrative limits.

The RFC says this can be overcome by the judicious use of permissions on directory entries and by intelligent implementations of administrative limits on the number of records retrieved.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone may only take a few results at a time, sorting could help them sneak out a whole directory a few at a time. Administrators must watch for that and set permissions carefully.

items.label: timeLimitExceeded
items.desc: Time limit reached before sorting was completed.

items.label: strongAuthRequired
items.desc: Refused to return sorted results over an insecure protocol.

items.label: adminLimitExceeded
items.desc: Too many matching entries for the server to sort.

items.label: noSuchAttribute
items.desc: Unrecognized attribute type in a sort key.

items.label: inappropriateMatching
items.desc: Unrecognized or inappropriate matching rule in a sort key.

items.label: insufficientAccessRights
items.desc: Refused to return sorted results to this client.
